sentences.text: This animal possessed wide, strap-like paramedian scutes with grooves and pits forming radial patterns.
Large horns on the side scutes curved backward, a feature also seen in related typothoracines like Typothorax.
Each scute ended with a distinct knob that overlapped the one behind it.
This aetosaur was widely distributed across Germany, North America, and possibly parts of Gondwana.
Fossils were first identified in the Chinle Group of the southwestern United States in 1992.
The first specimens were collected in the Heslach area near Stuttgart, Germany.
For over a century, these best-known remains were wrongly thought to be phytosaur armor.
Scientists finally recognized it as an aetosaur in 1953 and formally named the new genus in 1985.
A complete skeleton, specimen SMNS 19003, was unearthed in 1945 from the Schlipf Quarry near Murrhardt.
It was a large, wide-bodied typothoracine aetosaur and serves as the namesake for the tribe Paratypothoracisini.
The species is classified within the family Stagonolepididae.
It belongs to the tribe Paratypothoracisini.
The fossil range of this genus is estimated to span from the Late Carnian to the Rhaetian.
It lived during the Norian stage, approximately 227.3 to 205.7 million years ago.
Remains have been found in the Sonsela Member of Petrified Forest National Park in Arizona and the Bluewater Creek Formation in western New Mexico.
Osteoderms have also been reported from the Norian-age Fleming Fjord Formation in Greenland, the Zarzaitine Series in Algeria, and an unverified site in India.
